q: What dose of dexamethasone is given for tonsillectomy?
why: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg plus ondansetron for PONV and swelling.

q: According to APAGBI, which children can be treated as day-case tonsillectomy in any hospital?
why: Over 1 year and 10 kg only in hospitals with HDU; lower threshold for referral with severe OSA.

q: What is the peak timing of secondary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage?
why: Secondary haemorrhage can occur up to day 28, peaking at days 5–10.

q: A child is bleeding after tonsillectomy. What fluid bolus and TXA dose are given?
why: Then cross-matched blood if needed; consultant anaesthetist and senior ENT present.

q: Why are two working suckers needed for a bleeding tonsil?
why: Also have smaller ETTs available because of oedema.

q: What position is a child with a bleeding tonsil recovered in?
why: Blood drains out of the mouth rather than into the airway.

q: In severe OSA, why is opioid use reduced?
o: Increased opioid sensitivity raises the risk of respiratory depression and obstruction
why: Use multimodal analgesia with rescue opioid only.

q: What is the commonest cause of OSA in children?
why: 70–90% due to enlarged adenoids and tonsils, peaking at 3–10 years.

q: What should be checked after the Boyle–Davis gag is placed?
o: Ventilation (chest rise and pressures) for kinking or displacement
why: The gag can compress or dislodge the airway device.

q: What rescue morphine dose is used after tonsillectomy?
why: Morphine 0.1 mg/kg if needed, after paracetamol and ibuprofen.
